*Equal contribution. Preprint. Correspondence: {lingzhiy,furongh}@umd.edu. \paperlink[home]Projecthttps://meta-square.github.io/ \affiliations\affmark1University of Maryland; \affmark2University of Washington; \affmark3University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign; \affmark4Scale AI; \apaffiliation \abstracttextHarness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness for the task agent that may overfits training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch, or rely on verifier feedback which is usually unavailable at test-time. We introduce Meta2, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta2 learns a textual Meta-Skill ℳ\mathcal{M} by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of ℳ\mathcal{M}, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only during training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine ℳ\mathcal{M} into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen ℳ\mathcal{M} with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit shapes the remainder of the same run, preserving its environment state and accumulated progress. This way, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while realized harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta2 achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.

Meta2: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents

Lingzhi Yuan\affmark1,*    Yiguang Cai\affmark2,*    Weize Liu\affmark1    Siqi Yang\affmark3    Feijiang Han\affmark1    \apauthorYongkyun Lee    Udari Madhushani Sehwag\affmark4    \apauthor[1]Furong Huang

1 Introduction

Long-horizon agents do not act through a model alone. They act through a harness: prompts that frame decisions, a context policy that preserves information, tools and hooks that enable actions, and checks for completion [35, 26, 45, 51]. These mechanisms are often fixed before execution, yet the need to adapt them emerges during execution. A missing tool becomes apparent when the agent tries to use it; an overlooked constraint may surface in an intermediate artifact; and a one-time warning may need to become a recurring check. A harness chosen in advance must anticipate such situations before the trajectory that exposes them exists.

Because different tasks expose different interface and control needs, hand-designed harnesses [5, 36, 49, 3] must either anticipate a wide range of situations or be specialized manually. Automatic harness optimization reduces this burden, but most methods still make their consequential choices outside the active run. Offline methods optimize prompts, memory, tools, workflows, or complete harness programs on training tasks and deploy one shared artifact [20, 24, 58, 50, 54, 56, 1, 60]. This shared artifact may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online methods adapt the harness after the target task becomes available. Some customize it from the target instruction before execution (pre-run) or revise it using feedback from completed attempts (after-run) [57, 39, 43]. Recent systems support within-run evolution by updating prompts, tools, skills, or memory during execution [18, 6, 47, 46]. Such within-run harness evolution can be viewed as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), where an agent improves not only its task behavior but also the system that shapes its subsequent behavior. Pre-run and after-run adaptation cannot apply an edit to the unfinished run in which the motivating evidence arises. Within-run evolution can respond to such evidence as it emerges, but the evolver still needs guidance on when and how to intervene. This raises our central design question: how can lessons learned from completed training runs guide selective edits during a new run, without accessing held-out verifier feedback or making one task’s correction persist into unrelated tasks?

This question is difficult because evolution during a run is a sequential decision under partial information. At a checkpoint, an evolver can observe the active trajectory and permitted workspace state, but not the run’s eventual verifier outcome. It must decide whether intervention is warranted, what harness component to change, and how to express the change. Acting can rescue a failing trajectory, but it can also interrupt productive work or introduce a new failure; sometimes the correct action is to do nothing. Offline supervision for learning such guidance is also coarse: a terminal pass or failure evaluates a sequence of checkpoint decisions jointly rather than identifying which individual edit helped or harmed. Finally, reasoning about every evolution decision from scratch adds online token, latency, and monetary cost.

We introduce Meta2, a precompute-and-reuse approach which moves offline optimization one level up. Rather than optimizing a shared harness, it precomputes reusable evolution knowledge to guide the task-local edits online. Offline, Meta2 learns a textual Meta-Skill ℳ\mathcal{M} from training trajectories and verifier outcomes. Online, each run starts from the same seed harness h(0)h^{(0)}, and ℳ\mathcal{M} stays fixed across runs. A task agent executes normally; at checkpoints, a separate evolver uses ℳ\mathcal{M} and active-run evidence ℐ(k)\mathcal{I}^{(k)} to choose KEEP or EVOLVE​(δ(k))\textup{{EVOLVE}}(\delta^{(k)}). An edit δ(k)\delta^{(k)} is applied through a notice, instruction update, hook, or tool channel, and affects only the remainder of the current run. The task agent then continues with the same environment state and partial trajectory. Thus, the Meta-Skill is reused across tasks, while harness edits remain local to the run and are discarded when each run ends. Figure 1 illustrates this process.

The Meta-Skill is learned from comparisons of rollout outcomes rather than successful traces alone. For each training task, we run the same task agent under three conditions: A, without an evolver; B, with an evolver guided by the current version of ℳ\mathcal{M}; and C, with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only during training. A–B comparisons show when runs with the current evolver succeed or fail relative to runs without it; B–C comparisons reveal both recoveries missed by the current evolver and cases where verifier-informed evolution is associated with worse outcomes. These contrasts provide directional evidence to act, avoid, or hold without establishing the causal effect of any single checkpoint decision. Across training batches, REFLECT extracts lessons from these comparisons, AGGREGATE merges recurring patterns across tasks and removes instance-specific details, and UPDATE revises ℳ\mathcal{M}. During online evolution, ℳ\mathcal{M} is never updated with held-out verifier outcomes or task-specific edits.

We evaluate Meta2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1. With GPT-5.6-Terra, it achieves the highest performance among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. It also ranks first on Terminal-Bench with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, scoring 77.67%. Ablations show gains from adding the online evolver and further gains from contrastive Meta-Skill learning. We also report one-time offline construction and online deployment costs separately and examine how checkpoint frequency trades responsiveness for cost. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We formulate harness evolution by edit timing, available evidence and the executions affected. This taxonomy distinguishes offline optimization from pre-run, within-run, and after-run online adaptation.

  2. 2.

    We develop Meta2, a hybrid harness evolution paradigm which moves offline optimization from a shared harness to reusable evolution knowledge and uses that knowledge to guide task-local harness edits within a run.

  3. 3.

    We evaluate performance, cost, component contributions, and checkpoint-frequency sensitivity on two long-horizon benchmarks, with an additional backbone evaluation on Terminal-Bench.

2 Background: Harness Evolution

Task execution through a harness. (1) A task instance ξ=(x,ℰx,Vx)∼𝒟\xi=(x,\mathcal{E}_{x},V_{x})\sim\mathcal{D} comprises a public instruction xx, an interactive environment ℰx\mathcal{E}_{x}, and a verifier VxV_{x} whose criteria and outcome need not be observable to the agent or the evolver. (2) A task agent combines a model parameterized by θ\theta with a harness hth_{t}, comprising prompts, context policy, tools, skills, memory, and hooks that shape execution by, for example, preserving constraints, enabling actions, and validating artifacts. (3) At environment step tt, ℰx\mathcal{E}_{x} has state sts_{t}, including the current workspace and task artifacts, and emits an observation oto_{t}. Conditioned on the instruction, interaction history, and active harness, the agent selects an action according to at∼πθ(⋅∣x,τ≤t,ht)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\,\cdot\mid x,\tau_{\leq t},h_{t}\right), where τ≤t=(o1,a1,…,at−1,ot)\tau_{\leq t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t}). The environment transitions via Px(⋅∣st,at)P_{x}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}), and the verifier returns y=Vx​(sT)y=V_{x}(s_{T}) at termination.

Harness Evolution. To improve the performance of a task agent under an initial harness, we let an evolver gg revise it from evidence. Starting from a seed harness h(0)h^{(0)}, decision k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\ldots,K\} proposes and applies an edit:

δ(k)∼g(⋅∣h(k−1),ℐ(k)),h(k)=Apply(h(k−1),δ(k)),\delta^{(k)}\sim g\!\left(\,\cdot\mid h^{(k-1)},\mathcal{I}^{(k)}\right),\qquad h^{(k)}=\operatorname{Apply}\!\left(h^{(k-1)},\delta^{(k)}\right), (1)

where ℐ(k)\mathcal{I}^{(k)} is the evidence available to this decision, ℳ\mathcal{M} is reusable knowledge about when and how edits help or harm (possibly empty), h(k)h^{(k)} is the harness after decision kk, and a null edit sets h(k)=h(k−1)h^{(k)}=h^{(k-1)}. We evaluate harness evolution by Vx​(sT)V_{x}(s_{T}) on held-out tasks.

Offline evolution applies (1) on a training set 𝒮tr\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{tr}} before any target task is observed. Its evidence consists of completed training trajectories and their verifier outcomes, and it outputs a single harness h⋆h^{\star} shared by all target tasks. This amortizes experience across training tasks, but h⋆h^{\star} is fixed once execution begins: it cannot react to evidence revealed during a target run, and its persistent edits may overgeneralize beyond the failures that motivated them.

Online evolution applies (1) after the target task becomes available. There are three deployment-time settings, distinguished by when an edit is selected and which executions it affects: pre-run selects edits before execution (t=0t=0), using the target instruction and initial environment information to adapt the harness for the upcoming run; within-run selects edits at checkpoints during execution, using the partial trajectory and permitted workspace observations to adapt the harness for the remainder of the active run; and after-run selects edits once an attempt terminates, using completed trajectories and outcome feedback when available to adapt the harness for subsequent attempts or tasks. Only within-run evolution can respond while the motivating attempt is unfinished, but its decisions cannot depend on that attempt’s eventual verifier outcome. Appendix Table 7 compares the two instantiations of (1), which differ in available evidence and edit lifetime.

The two regimes are complementary. Offline evolution has verified training experience but cannot observe the target run, whereas within-run online evolution observes the target run but may lack reusable guidance from verified training experiences. This raises the question of whether verified offline experience can guide online edits without carrying tasks-specific edits across runs.

3 Meta2: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Evolution

Meta2 answers this question by moving the offline stage one level up. Instead of optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable evolution Meta-Skill ℳ\mathcal{M} from training trajectories and verifier feedback. At deployment, ℳ\mathcal{M} is frozen, and the evolver decides each within-run edit conditioned on it: δ(k)∼g(,⋅∣h(k−1),ℐ(k),ℳ)\delta^{(k)}\sim g(,\cdot\mid h^{(k-1)},\mathcal{I}^{(k)},\mathcal{M}). The Meta-Skill is reused across tasks, while each edit affects only its active run. As shown in Figure 2, Meta2 has three main components: a checkpoint-based interface for within-run evolution, an offline procedure that learns ℳ\mathcal{M}, and a deployment protocol that reuses ℳ\mathcal{M} without held-out verifier feedback.

3.1 Online Component: Checkpoint-Based Harness Evolution

Challenge: intervene without restarting. The evolver must decide whether and how to intervene before an active attempt ends, without resetting its environment, discarding its trajectory, or taking over its actions. Meta2 therefore separates two roles instantiated from the same frozen language model. The task agent starts from a minimal seed harness h(0)h^{(0)} and follows πθ\pi_{\theta}, while the evolver gg observes the run at checkpoints and may edit the harness.

Checkpoint information. Let ω(k)\omega^{(k)} denote the permitted read-only workspace observations obtained at checkpoint kk which may be empty. The evolver also receives the newly accumulated trajectory Δ​τ(k)\Delta\tau^{(k)} while retaining its preceding checkpoint conversation. Its information therefore accumulates as

ℐ(k)={(x,Δ​τ(1),ω(1)),k=1,ℐ(k−1)⊕(Δ​τ(k),ω(k),σ(k−1)),1<k≤K.\mathcal{I}^{(k)}=\begin{cases}\bigl(x,\Delta\tau^{(1)},\omega^{(1)}\bigr),&k=1,\\ \mathcal{I}^{(k-1)}\oplus\bigl(\Delta\tau^{(k)},\omega^{(k)},\sigma^{(k-1)}\bigr),&1<k\leq K.\end{cases} (2)

where ⊕\oplus denotes chronological append and σ(k−1)\sigma^{(k-1)} records whether the preceding edit was loaded, retained, or rolled back. The trajectory deltas reconstruct τ≤tk\tau_{\leq t_{k}}, while ω(k)\omega^{(k)} and σ(k−1)\sigma^{(k-1)} provide workspace observations and previous-edit status. Appendix Table 7 summarizes the available evidence across evolution regimes.

Decision and continuation. At checkpoint kk, the evolver makes a binary top-level decision:

u(k)∈{KEEP,EVOLVE​(δ(k))}.u^{(k)}\in\left\{\textup{{KEEP}},\textup{{EVOLVE}}\bigl(\delta^{(k)}\bigr)\right\}. (3)

KEEP sets h(k)=h(k−1)h^{(k)}=h^{(k-1)} and continues execution; EVOLVE applies δ(k)\delta^{(k)} through a bounded notice, instruction update, hook, or tool channel. At the terminal checkpoint, triggered by the task agent’s completion claim, the evolver also receives automatically collected workspace state. The action space remains unchanged: KEEP accepts the artifact, whereas EVOLVE applies a bounded correction and sends the task agent back for more work. This follows Equation 1 as the same-run loop (h(k−1),ℐ(k))→u(k)→h(k)\bigl(h^{(k-1)},\mathcal{I}^{(k)}\bigr)\!\rightarrow\!u^{(k)}\!\rightarrow\!h^{(k)}. Appendix B.2 specifies the checkpoint schedule, observation permissions, terminal state, and edit semantics.

3.2 Offline Component: Precomputing Reusable Evolution Knowledge

Challenge: learn checkpoint guidance from terminal outcomes. At deployment, the evolver must choose whether and how to edit using evidence available during the run, without held-out verifier feedback. Offline, the verifier supplies an outcome only after the entire run, evaluating a sequence of checkpoint decisions jointly. A passing or failing rollout therefore does not identify which intervention helped, harmed, or was unnecessary. Even when a useful intervention is found, its lessons must be separated from task-specific details before they can transfer.

Optimize the knowledge, not a single harness. We hold the language model, seed harness, checkpoint interface, and edit channels fixed, and optimize only the evolver’s reusable knowledge ℳ\mathcal{M}. This Meta-Skill links observable execution conditions to three guidance types: act supports an EVOLVE decision, hold supports KEEP, and avoid rules out a specific intervention even when another edit may remain appropriate. The evolver uses this guidance to decide whether and how to edit the harness during a new run. The offline output is therefore reusable decision knowledge rather than a universal harness or a predetermined edit. Offline optimization therefore transfers decision knowledge, not a universal harness or a predetermined edit. Appendix B.1 gives the full offline construction algorithm, and Appendix I specifies the entry fields and content of the Meta-Skill.

A/B/C rollouts make terminal feedback informative. For each training task, we run the same task agent with the same language model and seed harness under three conditions: A, without an evolver; B, with an evolver guided by the current version of ℳ\mathcal{M}; and C, with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only during training. A–B contrasts compare outcomes with and without the current evolver, whereas B–C contrasts reveal additional recoveries or failures under verifier-informed evolution. Condition C is particularly useful on difficult tasks, where both A and B may fail and their comparison provides no successful examples. By giving the evolver privileged verifier information, C can produce successful rollouts that allow B–C contrasts to reveal recovery strategies missed by the current evolver. To prevent these recoveries from relying on direct verifier leakage, the condition-C evolver’s system prompt strictly prohibits passing privileged verifier information to the task agent. We also audit condition-C trajectories after execution and exclude those that violate this restriction from contrast construction and Meta-Skill learning.

Five contrast directions. B-pass/A-fail and C-pass/B-fail provide act evidence for potentially useful interventions and recoveries missed by the current evolver, respectively. B-fail/A-pass and C-fail/B-pass provide avoid evidence for potential harm from current and verifier-informed interventions, respectively. A-pass/B-pass provides hold evidence from cases where the task agent succeeds with or without an evolver. These comparisons give each candidate lesson a direction but do not establish the causal effect of a single checkpoint decision.

From task-level contrasts to reusable rules. We process training tasks in batches. For batch rr, REFLECT inspects each retained contrastive group and writes candidate entries following the predefined entry schema for each task; AGGREGATE merges recurring patterns across tasks and removes instance-specific details; and UPDATE adds, merges, refines, or deletes entries relative to ℳ(r−1)\mathcal{M}^{(r-1)}. Let 𝒢(r)\mathcal{G}^{(r)} denote the retained contrastive groups and V(r)V^{(r)} their privileged training-time verifier information. The update is

ℳ(r)=fupd​(ℳ(r−1),fagg​(fref​(𝒢(r),V(r)))).\mathcal{M}^{(r)}=f_{\mathrm{upd}}\!\left(\mathcal{M}^{(r-1)},f_{\mathrm{agg}}\!\left(f_{\mathrm{ref}}\!\left(\mathcal{G}^{(r)},V^{(r)}\right)\right)\right). (4)

All three stages use LLM calls to the same base model used by the task agent and evolver. After the final batch, the resulting Meta-Skill is frozen for deployment, where it guides edits selected from evidence in each active run.

3.3 Deployment Component: Frozen Knowledge and Task-Local Edits

Challenge: reuse without contamination. At deployment, the evolver receives no held-out verifier feedback to confirm whether a task-local edit helped the active run. An edit motivated by one task’s trajectory may also be inappropriate for another, so carrying it forward risks imposing task-specific changes on unrelated runs. We therefore reuse the offline Meta-Skill but reset the harness to the same h(0)h^{(0)} at the start of every new run.

Freeze globally, adapt locally. At deployment, the learned Meta-Skill ℳ\mathcal{M} is frozen, and every run starts from the same seed harness h(0)h^{(0)}. At checkpoint kk, the evolver decides an edit conditioned on both ℳ\mathcal{M} and active-run evidence: δ(k)∼g(⋅∣h(k−1),ℐ(k),ℳ)\delta^{(k)}\sim g(\cdot\mid h^{(k-1)},\mathcal{I}^{(k)},\mathcal{M}). This extends (1) by explicitly conditioning gg on the reusable knowledge learned offline. The checkpoint interface remains unchanged: KEEP leaves the harness unchanged, while EVOLVE applies δ(k)\delta^{(k)} and resumes the task agent with the same environment state and partial trajectory, as described in Section 3.1. Each edit affects only the remainder of the active run and is discarded when that run ends. Online decisions, task-specific edits, and outcomes are not written back to ℳ\mathcal{M}; neither held-out verifier feedback nor an LLM-as-a-judge signal is used to update it. The next run therefore reuses the same Meta-Skill and starts again from h(0)h^{(0)}, carrying over evolution knowledge but none of the preceding run’s harness edits.

4 Experiments

We organize the evaluation around four questions. RQ1 asks whether Meta2 improves held-out task performance. RQ2 examines whether the offline cost of precomputing reusable evolution knowledge is justified when reused at deployment. RQ3 studies the tradeoff between checkpoint responsiveness and online cost. RQ4 identifies which method components account for the gains.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate Meta2 on two challenging long-horizon benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1 [32] and DeepSWE 1.1 [12]. We randomly split each benchmark into training and test sets at a 1:2 ratio. We report mean@5 over five independent runs on every held-out Terminal-Bench task and mean@3 over three independent runs on every held-out DeepSWE task. Appendix C.1 provides dataset splits and evaluation details.

Baselines. We compare Meta2 against three groups of baselines: (1) human-designed harnesses: NexAU [33], Codex CLI [36], mini-swe-agent [49], Pi agent [5], and DeepSeek Harness [3]; (2) self-evolution methods: ACE [61], Training-free GRPO [2], and ReasoningBank [38]; and (3) harness-evolution methods: AHE [24], Meta-Harness [20], and Continual Harness [18]. All self-evolution and harness-evolution methods start from the same NexAU seed harness, denoted h(0)h^{(0)} for Meta2.

Implementation details. Self-evolution baselines construct their experience libraries on the training split; ReasoningBank and ACE can further update their libraries as test evaluation proceeds. AHE uses best-of-two proposals for five iterations, while Meta-Harness uses one proposal per iteration for ten iterations. Both deploy the harness with the highest training score at test-time. Continual Harness starts from its training-evolved harness and retains edits made during test evaluation, whereas Meta2 starts every run from h(0)h^{(0)} with a frozen Meta-Skill. No method that adapts at test time is allowed to observe held-out verifier outcomes. Appendix C.2 gives the detailed full settings.

LLM backbones. Our primary experiments use GPT-5.6-Terra [37] with medium reasoning effort. We additionally evaluate Terminal-Bench 2.1 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 [4] at high reasoning effort. Within each backbone setting, all agent roles across all compared systems use the same underlying model. We route all calls through one LiteLLM proxy and compute cost from the per-call charges in its response headers.

4.2 RQ1: Does Meta2 Improve Task Performance?

Primary comparison. With GPT-5.6-Terra, Meta2 achieves the highest performance point estimate among evaluated methods on both benchmarks, reaching 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1 as shown in Table 1. These correspond to gains of 14.67 and 9.77 percentage points over the shared NexAU seed harness, compared with 7.00 and 2.66 points for Meta-Harness, the strongest harness-evolution baseline. All evolution-based methods improve over the seed on Terminal-Bench. On DeepSWE, however, ReasoningBank, ACE, and Continual Harness fall below the seed, while AHE only matches it. In contrast, Meta2 still retains a 9.77-point improvement, suggesting that condition C can supply useful training examples on difficult tasks where other evolution methods fail to improve.

Robustness across backbones. Table 2 repeats the Terminal-Bench evaluation with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 as the backbone. Meta2 again achieves the highest performance, reaching 77.67% and outperforming the shared NexAU seed and Continual Harness by 7.67 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively. The three self-evolution baselines score below the seed; AHE and Meta-Harness improve by 1.33 and 1.00 points, while Continual Harness improves by 4.67 points. We construct a separate Meta-Skill for each backbone, so this experiment evaluates robustness across backbones rather than zero-shot transfer of a frozen Meta-Skill between models.

4.3 RQ2: Is Precomputation Cost-Effective When Reused?

Cost comparison. Table 1 separates one-time offline construction cost from online deployment cost. Compared with the offline harness-evolution methods AHE and Meta-Harness, Meta2 achieves higher performance at lower full cost on both benchmarks. Its full costs are $174.91 on Terminal-Bench and $367.86 on DeepSWE, compared with $248.35 and $862.89 for AHE, and $198.85 and $870.75 for Meta-Harness. With the highest observed performance among evaluated methods, Meta2 lies on the performance–cost Pareto frontier on both benchmarks, as shown in Figure 9 in Appendix E.2.

Reusable precomputation. Compared with Continual Harness, another online harness evolution method, Meta2 incurs higher offline construction costs: $110.19 versus $28.75 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and $238.52 versus $46.11 on DeepSWE 1.1. However, it achieves higher performance at lower online costs: $64.72 versus $83.48 and $129.34 versus $155.61, respectively. The offline construction cost is a one-time investment: the resulting Meta-Skill can be reused across subsequent tasks and runs without reconstruction, so additional deployments incur only online cost. The construction cost is therefore amortized over a larger workload as the Meta-Skill is reused.

4.4 RQ3: How Does Checkpoint Frequency Trade Responsiveness for Cost?

Checkpoint-interval sensitivity. Figure 4.4 varies the fixed checkpoint interval LL on Terminal-Bench 2.1. A moderate interval of L=5L=5 achieves the highest performance (81.00%) and the best observed performance–cost balance, at an online cost of $64.72. More frequent checkpoints increase cost without improving performance: L=3L=3 and L=1L=1 cost $74.22 and $83.41 but score 80.33% and 79.00% respectively. Longer intervals reduce cost modestly, reaching $59.10 at L=11L=11 and the performance compromises as well. Importantly, Meta2 outperforms every baseline at every evaluated value of LL, showing that its advantage is robust to the checkpoint schedule.

4.5 RQ4: Which Components Produce the Gains?

Component contributions. Figure 4 compares five settings. The first four compare the task agent alone, the task agent with an online evolver without any distilled knowledge, and the two-agent system with either a self-distilled or contrastive Meta-Skill. Their Terminal-Bench/DeepSWE scores are 66.33/34.67, 74.67/36.44, 77.00/35.56, and 81.00/44.44, respectively. Adding the online evolver improves performance on both benchmarks, while the self-distilled Meta-Skill improves Terminal-Bench but slightly reduces DeepSWE performance. Contrastive Meta-Skill learning improves over self-distillation by 4.00 and 8.88 percentage points, respectively, highlighting its value particularly on harder tasks.

Resetting between tasks. The fifth setting starts each new task from the harness produced by the preceding task, retaining all online edits rather than resetting to h(0)h^{(0)}. Performance falls from 81.00% to 78.33% on Terminal-Bench and from 44.44% to 39.11% on DeepSWE. Online edits are derived from the trajectory of the active task and may therefore encode task-specific interventions that do not transfer to the next task. These results support reusing the frozen Meta-Skill while resetting the harness for each new task, so that task-specific edits remain local to the run that produced them.

5 Related Work

Offline harness evolution. Using the taxonomy in Section 2 and Appendix Table 7, we group prior work by edit selection time. Offline methods optimize the system around a frozen model on training tasks and deploy the result as a fixed artifact. Early work optimizes prompts and LM pipelines [48, 19, 56, 1], and later work searches over code-defined agent systems and workflows [11, 60]. For long-horizon agents, recent methods evolve the harness itself: they rewrite the scaffold [59], propose harnesses from prior code, scores, and traces [20], tie edits to checkable predictions [24], or retain regression-tested edits [58]. Analyses suggest that many of these gains compensate for recoverable execution defects of the underlying model [50]. In all cases, the deployed harness h⋆h^{\star} is shared across held-out runs and cannot react to evidence revealed during a run. Meta2 also learns from completed training runs, but it freezes reusable evolution knowledge ℳ\mathcal{M} rather than a harness, so the same ℳ\mathcal{M} can support different edits in runs.

Online harness evolution: pre-run and after-run. Pre-run methods adapt the harness once the target task is known but before execution begins; for example, JIT-Agent synthesizes a task-specific harness for each incoming task [57]. After-run methods adapt from completed attempts. Reflexion [40] and Harness-R1 [39] use feedback or failure trajectories to improve later attempts on the same task, while Dynamic Cheatsheet, ACE, and TTHE update memory, guidance, or harness programs over a stream of tasks [42, 61, 34]. In both settings, the edit either precedes the evidence that execution reveals or benefits only later attempts or tasks, and after-run selection often relies on completed-run feedback or proxy signals. Meta2 instead edits the run in which the evidence appears, without observing that run’s verifier outcome.

Online harness evolution: within-run. The closest setting adapts the harness during an uninterrupted run. Continual Harness refines prompts, skills, and memory inside a reset-free episode [18]; PILOT uses a supervisor to steer an active worker [47]; and Live-SWE-agent modifies its own tools while solving a task [46]. These systems show that within-run adaptation is feasible and useful, but they decide when and how to intervene without guidance. Meta2 supplies this guidance. Offline, A/B/C outcome contrasts produce a textual Meta-Skill that records when to act, hold, or avoid an intervention. Online, an evolver applies this frozen knowledge to the active run without held-out verifier feedback. Table 6 and 7 in Appendix G summarizes the distinction: Meta2 is a hybrid that evolves reusable knowledge offline and task-local edits within the run.

6 Conclusion

Meta2 moves offline optimization one level up, learning reusable knowledge for harness evolution instead of a fixed harness. Offline rollout contrasts produce a Meta-Skill that is frozen at deployment; an online evolver uses it together with active-run evidence to decide harness edits that remain local to each run. Meta2 achieves 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra, and 77.67% on Terminal-Bench with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. Ablations support contrastive Meta-Skill learning and resetting the harness between tasks. These results support a simple principle: precompute how to adapt, then adapt locally as the task unfolds.

Appendix A Notation

Table 3 summarizes the core notation used in the main text and Appendix B.

Appendix B Algorithmic Details

This appendix specifies the offline Meta-Skill construction procedure and the online checkpoint evolution loop described in Section 3. Prompt templates are provided separately in Appendix H.

B.1 Offline Meta-Skill Construction

For each training task ξ\xi, let ℛξq\mathcal{R}^{q}_{\xi} denote the rollout records under condition q∈{A,B,C}q\in\{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B},\mathrm{C}\}, including trajectories, terminal verifier outcomes, and intervention logs when applicable. Condition A uses the task agent alone; condition B uses an evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill; and condition C uses an evolver with privileged training-time verifier information. Condition-A and condition-C records are collected once and reused, whereas condition-B records are collected with ℳ(r−1)\mathcal{M}^{(r-1)} for batch rr.

Contrast construction. BUILDCONTRASTS forms five outcome-conditioned directions: B-pass/A-fail and C-pass/B-fail provide act evidence; B-fail/A-pass and C-fail/B-pass provide avoid evidence; and A-pass/B-pass provides hold evidence. These contrasts provide directional evidence for candidate lessons, without identifying the causal effect of an individual checkpoint decision. Condition-C rollouts are excluded if privileged verifier information is passed to the task agent.

Reflection, aggregation, and update. For each retained group GG, V⁡(G)V(G) denotes the privileged training-time verifier information associated with its task. REFLECT writes candidate entries following the predefined Meta-Skill schema. AGGREGATE groups entries by observable trigger, removes instance-specific details, and requires support from at least two distinct tasks. UPDATE adds, merges, refines, or deletes entries while preserving provenance. The resulting Meta-Skill is frozen before held-out evaluation.

B.2 Online Checkpoint Evolution

Every held-out run starts from the same seed harness h(0)h^{(0)} and frozen Meta-Skill ℳ\mathcal{M}. Checkpoints follow the configured schedule with interval LL, and a completion claim triggers a terminal checkpoint. The evolver retains its checkpoint conversation within the active run, but receives neither held-out verifier contents nor verifier outcomes.

Decision and edit semantics. DECIDE denotes the evolver’s top-level KEEP or EVOLVE(δ(k))(\delta^{(k)}) decision, conditioned on the current harness, accumulated checkpoint evidence, and frozen Meta-Skill. The edit contract specifies the supporting evidence, target, content, channel, lifetime, validation, and rollback behavior. An edit that fails validation is rejected without changing the harness.

Continuation and isolation. Accepted edits are applied through a bounded notice, instruction update, hook, or tool channel. A terminal KEEP accepts the artifact; a valid terminal EVOLVE applies a correction and returns the task agent to the same run, subject to the send-back budget. Neither ordinary checkpoints nor terminal send-backs reset the environment or discard accumulated progress. Harness edits and checkpoint conversations remain local to the run and are discarded afterward. The Meta-Skill is never updated online, and the held-out verifier is used only for evaluation after termination.

Appendix C Detailed Experimental Setup

C.1 Datasets and Splits

We evaluate on Terminal-Bench 2.1 [32] and DeepSWE 1.1 [12], which assess terminal-based task execution and repository-level software engineering, respectively. Their main characteristics are summarized below.

  • •

    Terminal-Bench 2.1. This benchmark contains 89 tasks requiring agents to complete complex workflows in containerized command-line environments. Tasks span software engineering, system administration, data processing, model training, security, and scientific computing. Each task provides an instruction, an execution environment, and automated verification of the resulting artifacts or system state.

  • •

    DeepSWE 1.1. This benchmark contains 113 original software-engineering tasks across 91 open-source repositories in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript, and Rust. Tasks require agents to understand existing codebases and implement changes such as new features, bug fixes, and extensions to existing interfaces. Hand-written verifiers assess software behavior rather than requiring a particular implementation.

For each benchmark, we randomly partition the tasks into training and test sets at an approximately 1:2 ratio and fix these splits across all methods and backbone settings. Table 4 reports the number of tasks in each split. Offline construction of experience libraries, evolved harnesses, and Meta-Skills uses only the corresponding training split. Held-out verifier contents and outcomes are unavailable to methods during test-time execution.

Evaluation protocol. We perform five independent runs per held-out Terminal-Bench task and three per held-out DeepSWE task, reporting mean@5 and mean@3, respectively. For each task, we average its binary verifier outcomes across repeated runs and then average these task-level scores over the test set. This yields 300 evaluated runs per method on Terminal-Bench and 225 on DeepSWE within each backbone setting. All methods within a benchmark/backbone setting use the same held-out tasks and repetition count.

Execution environment. Task execution takes place in cloud-based sandboxes provisioned through E2B. These sandboxes host the task environments and workspaces in which agents execute commands, inspect files, and produce task artifacts. For Meta2, checkpoint interventions and terminal send-backs continue within the same sandbox, preserving the active environment state and accumulated task progress.

C.2 Baselines and Setup

We compare against three groups of baselines: human-designed harnesses (NexAU [33], Codex CLI [36], mini-swe-agent [49], Pi agent [5], and DeepSeek Harness [3]), self-evolution methods (ReasoningBank [38], ACE [61], and TF-GRPO [2]), and harness-evolution methods (AHE [24], Meta-Harness [20], and Continual Harness [18]). All self-evolution and harness-evolution methods start from the same NexAU seed harness.

Training-time construction. ACE, TF-GRPO, AHE, and Meta-Harness use five rollouts per training task for experience collection or candidate evaluation. AHE uses best-of-two candidate proposals for five iterations on each benchmark. Meta-Harness proposes one candidate per iteration for ten iterations. Both AHE and Meta-Harness evaluate each candidate with five trials per training task and deploy the harness with the highest training score. ReasoningBank and Continual Harness do not originally include a separate offline training stage. To give them access to the same training split, we add a pre-deployment stage in which ReasoningBank accumulates experience and Continual Harness refines its harness on training tasks. Both methods use one rollout per training task and process training tasks in windows of eight. Their resulting experience library or evolved harness initializes test-time evaluation.

Test-time adaptation and persistence. ACE and ReasoningBank continue updating their experience libraries as test evaluation proceeds, retaining these updates across runs. Continual Harness likewise continues refining its harness and retains its edits across runs, including edits accumulated during the training stage. Its refinement schedule uses a 25-step warmup, followed by refinement every 25 steps through step 200 and every 100 steps thereafter, with each refinement conditioned on the most recent 50 steps. TF-GRPO, AHE, and Meta-Harness freeze their learned artifacts after training and perform no further evolution during test evaluation. In contrast, Meta2 reuses a frozen Meta-Skill but resets the task-agent harness to h(0)h^{(0)} at the start of every run. Its online harness edits affect only the active run and are discarded afterward. No method that adapts at test time can access held-out verifier contents or outcomes.

C.3 Implementation Details of Meta2

Offline Meta-Skill construction. For each benchmark/backbone setting, we construct a separate Meta-Skill using only the corresponding training split and freeze it before evaluation. The task agent and evolver use the same frozen language model, and offline optimization changes only the Meta-Skill while holding the seed harness, checkpoint interface, and edit channels fixed. We collect rollouts under three conditions: task-agent-only execution (A), evolution guided by the current Meta-Skill (B), and evolution with privileged training-time verifier information (C). The condition-C evolver is instructed not to pass privileged verifier information to the task agent, and rollouts that fail the subsequent leakage audit are excluded from contrast construction. Outcome-conditioned A–B and B–C comparisons provide directional evidence for candidate act, hold, and avoid entries. These entries are reflected from task-level contrasts, aggregated across tasks, and used to update the Meta-Skill through the procedure in Appendix B.1.

Online execution. Every test run starts from the same NexAU seed harness h(0)h^{(0)} and the frozen Meta-Skill constructed for its benchmark/backbone setting. The evolver is first called immediately after the task agent’s first step, providing an early opportunity to guide execution and avoid unnecessary subsequent exploration. Regular checkpoints use a five-step interval, and a terminal checkpoint is triggered when the task agent stops calling tools and prepares to submit its result. At each checkpoint, the evolver receives the newly accumulated trajectory delta, permitted read-only workspace observations, and, after the first checkpoint, the preceding-edit status. It retains its checkpoint conversation within the active run and chooses KEEP or EVOLVE conditioned on this accumulated evidence and the frozen Meta-Skill. Available edit channels are a one-turn notice, a persistent instruction update, a read-only hook, and an added tool. At the terminal checkpoint, the evolver additionally receives mechanically collected state for task-referenced paths, created or modified files, newly listening TCP ports, and processes started during the run that remain alive. A terminal KEEP accepts the artifact, whereas EVOLVE applies a bounded correction and sends the task agent back for additional work, subject to a bounded send-back budget. All interventions continue within the same task-agent run and sandbox, preserving the environment state and accumulated trajectory. Harness edits and checkpoint conversations are discarded when the run ends. Test-time trajectories, edits, and outcomes never update the Meta-Skill, and held-out verifier contents and outcomes remain unavailable to the evolver.

Appendix D Case Study

Each figure compares two runs of the same task: one with an evolver operating without a Meta-Skill and one with an evolver guided by the learned Meta-Skill. Both runs use the same initial task-agent harness, language model (GPT-5.6 Terra), and checkpoint schedule, with an initial checkpoint after the first agent step, regular checkpoints every five agent steps, and a terminal checkpoint before submission. Each lane spans the observed number of task-agent steps, and checkpoint markers indicate KEEP or EVOLVE. The latter includes notices, persistent instruction or hook updates, tool additions, and terminal send-backs. Figures 6–8 illustrate the three Meta-Skill entry types: act, where guidance supports an early or mid-run intervention; avoid, where guidance discourages a particular intervention; and hold, where guidance supports leaving the harness unchanged. Entry identifiers are specific to each benchmark’s Meta-Skill.

Appendix E Supplementary Experiment Results

E.1 Mean and Standard Deviation Across Repeated Runs

Table 5 reports mean performance and sample standard deviation across repeated evaluation runs. Each repetition covers the full held-out task set: 60 tasks for Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 75 tasks for DeepSWE 1.1. We compute the percentage of tasks passed in each repetition, then report the mean and sample standard deviation over five repetitions for Terminal-Bench and three for DeepSWE. Standard deviations are expressed in percentage points and describe variation across repetitions.

E.2 Cost–Performance Pareto Frontier

Figure 9 compares held-out performance against full cost for GPT-5.6-Terra on both benchmarks. Full cost includes offline construction, where applicable, and online execution over the complete held-out evaluation. A method is Pareto dominated if another method has no higher cost and no lower performance, with a strict improvement in at least one dimension. The dashed lines connect the non-dominated point estimates.

Meta2 lies on the Pareto frontier and achieves the highest performance point estimate on both benchmarks. It also dominates AHE and Meta-Harness, attaining higher performance at lower full cost. Lower-cost human-designed harnesses remain on both frontiers, while Continual Harness and TF-GRPO provide intermediate cost–performance tradeoffs on Terminal-Bench. Thus, Meta2 extends the frontier toward higher performance while retaining alternatives with lower total expenditure. These comparisons use the evaluation sizes reported in Appendix C.1; the contribution of one-time offline construction to full cost depends on the number of subsequent runs.

Appendix F Additional Discussion

F.1 Limitations

Interpretation of outcome contrasts. The A/B/C comparisons provide run-level evidence for evolution guidance rather than causal estimates of individual checkpoint decisions. Because independently sampled trajectories may diverge before an intervention, differences in terminal outcomes cannot be attributed to a single edit. Accordingly, the Meta-Skill records guidance grounded in observed contrasts, and the evolver assesses its applicability using evidence from the active run. Controlled comparisons that resume from a shared checkpoint state would enable more precise attribution.

Deployment cost and intervention timing. The evolver introduces additional model calls, and its deployment cost depends on checkpoint frequency and the extent of intervention. Our checkpoint-frequency study examines this tradeoff, while hold and avoid guidance supports selective intervention. Bounded edit channels, validation, and rollback further constrain changes to the active harness. These mechanisms do not guarantee that every intervention is useful or timely, leaving room for more efficient checkpoint scheduling and decision policies.

Scope of reusable guidance. Cross-task aggregation removes instance-specific details to produce guidance that can be reused across tasks. The resulting entries remain abstractions of the training evidence, and their applicability depends on whether the active run exhibits the relevant conditions. Support from multiple tasks and retained source examples aid interpretation and traceability, but do not establish applicability to all task distributions. Evaluating transfer under broader distribution shifts is a useful direction for future work.

Evaluation coverage. Our evaluation focuses on terminal and software-engineering tasks with inspectable artifacts and automatic verification. The results establish performance within these settings and the evaluated backbone configurations. Further evaluation is needed to assess applicability to domains with different interaction structures or less explicit completion criteria, such as embodied control and open-ended research.

F.2 Broader Impact and Safety

Online harness evolution may improve the reliability of long-horizon agents by allowing them to respond to tool failures, artifact errors, and evidence revealed during execution. A reusable Meta-Skill can support consistent intervention decisions when similar situations recur. Because harness edits influence subsequent agent behavior, deployment should account for tool permissions, the confidentiality of trajectory data, and the traceability of changes.

Our implementation restricts workspace inspection to permitted read-only observations and applies task-local edits through bounded channels with validation and rollback. The Meta-Skill remains frozen during deployment, and intervention logs record checkpoint decisions and harness changes. For broader deployment, we recommend least-privilege tool access, explicit edit scopes, versioned changes, and access-controlled audit logs. Edits that expand permissions or authorize external actions beyond the original task scope should require human approval. Privileged verifier information is used only during offline construction, with condition-C rollouts audited for leakage before inclusion in Meta-Skill learning.

F.3 Future Directions

One direction is to refine the Meta-Skill during deployment using reliable feedback from newly completed tasks. This could help the guidance adapt to changing task distributions, provided that updates distinguish reusable lessons from task-specific corrections and are validated before reuse. Such a protocol would require an explicit source of deployment feedback, separate from held-out verifier information reserved for evaluation.

A second direction is to replace fixed checkpoint intervals with an adaptive scheduling policy. The policy could use execution evidence and evolver uncertainty to determine when inspection is warranted, balancing timely intervention against monitoring cost. Further extensions include retrieving relevant entries from larger Meta-Skills, identifying situations not covered by existing guidance, and evaluating transfer across task-agent models and domains.

Appendix G Evolution Regimes and Related-Work Comparison

Table 6 summarizes the evolution regimes supported by representative methods. The four regime columns describe offline optimization and pre-run, within-run, and after-run evolution, following the definitions in Section 2. A checkmark denotes explicit support, a triangle denotes support restricted to particular modes or reuse of completed-run artifacts, and a cross denotes that the regime is not supported in the described protocol. The final column indicates whether deployment-time adaptation requires task-verifier feedback, including feedback used to select updates for subsequent runs. The comparison describes the original methods rather than the training-time adaptations introduced for our baseline evaluation.

The online evolution regimes are not mutually exclusive: a method may adapt before or during a run and also use completed-run evidence to update artifacts for subsequent tasks. For example, JIT-Agent generates a task-specific harness before execution and, in its streaming mode, uses the completed rollout’s reward, latency, and cost to update the harness bank. PILOT combines within-run steering and harness updates with verifier-based selection of which updates to retain across iterations. Continual Harness refines its harness within a run and retains the resulting harness in subsequent runs.

Table 7 summarizes harness evolution by decision timing, available evidence, and the executions affected by an update. Offline optimization uses training experience to construct an artifact shared across target runs, whereas online evolution adapts after the target task becomes available. The online settings differ in whether an update affects the upcoming run, the remainder of an active run, or subsequent attempts or tasks. The final row locates Meta2 within this taxonomy: the Meta-Skill ℳ\mathcal{M} is learned offline and reused across tasks, while checkpoint information ℐ(k)\mathcal{I}^{(k)} guides task-local edits δ(k)\delta^{(k)} during execution.

The UPDATE stage is invoked once per training batch to incorporate aggregated entries into the current Meta-Skill. It uses the shared system prompt in Appendix H.2 and the instructions below. Updates consider both new entries and entry-level feedback, while preserving identifiers, source support, and examples.

Appendix I Meta-Skill Structure and Content

I.1 Entry Structure

A Meta-Skill is a versioned textual library that guides harness evolution at checkpoints. Each entry associates an observable situation with guidance on whether and how to intervene. The evolver interprets these entries using evidence from the active run to select a task-local harness edit or leave the harness unchanged. We denote the frozen library by ℳ={ei}i=1N\mathcal{M}=\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, with the entry fields summarized in Table 8.

The When to refer field describes an observable condition at a level that permits reuse across tasks. Vague judgments such as “the approach looks wrong” provide little basis for matching an entry to checkpoint evidence. Conversely, exact file names, commands, packages, or expected answers tie a trigger to a particular instance. We therefore express triggers through observable relations, such as a claim contradicted by command output, repeated attempts that produce no new evidence, or an artifact inconsistent with the task agent’s completion claim. Task-specific details are confined to reference examples and internal provenance records. Construction metadata, including supporting task identifiers and candidate provenance, is retained separately to support aggregation and subsequent updates.

I.2 Content of Meta-Skills

Entries are organized by type and execution stage. The act entries describe situations in which training contrasts support an intervention, such as an unverified execution route, an unresolved contradiction, or an unsupported completion claim. The hold entries identify situations where the task agent is making progress or recovering without assistance. The avoid entries describe interventions associated with adverse outcomes, such as prematurely selecting an interpretation or redirecting a search that is still advancing. These types guide different aspects of a checkpoint decision: act supports a change, hold supports continuation, and avoid excludes a particular change while leaving other interventions available.

The execution-stage labels further specify when the guidance applies. Start entries concern early constraints, evidence preservation, and route selection. During entries concern evidence revealed as work proceeds, including progress, contradictions, and unverified behavior. End entries concern whether the delivered artifact and available validation support acceptance.

Cross-task aggregation retains reusable guidance supported by at least two distinct training tasks. Raw verifier text, hidden expected outputs, task solutions, and held-out information are excluded from the deployed guidance. At deployment, the frozen Meta-Skill is supplied directly in the evolver’s conversation. Entries labeled start are delivered in the first checkpoint message, while the remaining entries are included in the system prompt. All entries remain available in the evolver’s conversation at subsequent checkpoints. The evolver records the entry IDs it uses, or indicates that no entry applies, and grounds each decision in evidence from the active run. Checkpoint decisions, task-local edits, and test-time outcomes do not update the frozen library.
